title: What a seed bank remembers
bodyMd:
A hypothetical research team studying a grassland finds that the plants growing above ground in a dry year differ markedly from those growing after two wet years. An initial survey therefore suggests that several species disappeared during the drought and later recolonized the site. Yet soil samples collected during the drought contain viable seeds of some of the supposedly absent species. The team argues that a census of visible plants measures only the currently expressed portion of the community, not every species capable of contributing to its future composition.

That distinction does not make the soil seed bank a complete catalogue of the past. Species differ in how long their seeds survive, and some rely chiefly on vegetative reproduction. Moreover, the team’s germination experiment uses a particular combination of light, temperature, and moisture. A viable seed that requires different conditions may fail to germinate in the experiment. Consequently, the absence of a species from germinated samples cannot by itself establish the absence of viable seeds of that species from the sampled soil.

The researchers recommend combining above-ground surveys with several germination treatments and, where feasible, direct examination of seeds. The approaches answer overlapping but different questions. Above-ground surveys document realized establishment under recent conditions; germination trials reveal a portion of the latent capacity for establishment; direct examination may detect seeds without establishing their viability. A claim about community resilience should therefore specify which kind of evidence supports it. Finding dormant seeds suggests one route by which a community might recover, but does not guarantee that those seeds will germinate, survive, and reproduce after the next disturbance.
